sources.entry: PACELC theorem: "in case of network partitioning (P) in a distributed computer system, one has to choose between availability (A) and consistency (C) (as per the CAP theorem), but else (E), even when the system is running normally in the absence of partitions, one has to choose between latency (L) and consistency (C)."

summary.title: PACELC design principle
summary.one_liner: PACELC extends the CAP theorem by adding that even without network partitions, distributed databases must trade off latency against consistency, and it classifies systems into four PA/PC-EL/EC configurations.
takeaways: During a network partition, a system must choose between availability (A) and consistency (C), as in CAP.
Even when there is no partition (ELC), a replicated system must choose between latency (L) and consistency (C).
PACELC yields four configurations: PA/EL, PA/EC, PC/EL and PC/EC.
The page gives PACELC ratings for databases such as Cassandra, DynamoDB, MongoDB, PostgreSQL, and Cosmos DB.
summary.summary: This Wikipedia article describes the PACELC design principle, introduced by Daniel Abadi in 2010 and formalized in a 2012 paper, as an extension of CAP theorem. It explains the partition trade-off (A vs C) and the normal-operation latency vs consistency trade-off, then lists the four PACELC configurations and their developer implications. The article closes with a table and notes classifying many databases (Dynamo, Cassandra, DynamoDB, MongoDB, PostgreSQL, Couchbase, Hazelcast and others) by PACELC category, with references to the original papers and a formal proof from 2018.
